Respondent No. 2
Counsel for the Appellant(s) : Mr. Sidhant Kumar
Ms. Manya Chandok
Ms. Ekshha Kashyap for A-1 to A3
Counsel for the Respondent(s) : Mr. Sridhar Potaraju

JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by the Southern Power Distribution
Company of Andhra Pradesh Ltd. and others (collectively referred to as the
“Appellants”). The Appellants are aggrieved by the order dated 05.07.2021
passed by the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (“State
Commission”) in Original Petition (O.P.) No. 20 of 2020.
2. In the Impugned Order, the State Commission dealt with the status of the
Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 30.03.2017 executed between
Appellant No. 1- Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh
(APSPDCL) and Respondent No. 2 (M/s. Chaitanya Projects Ltd., herein after
briefly referred as M/s. Chaitanya). The State Commission declared the PPA
invalid and legally unenforceable on the ground that it lacked the mandatory
Page 2 of 6

Judgement in Appeal No. 456 of 2022
statutory approval required under Section 86(1) (b) of the Electricity Act, 2003. In
the same order, the State Commission, invoking Section 70 of the Contract Act,
1872, had directed APSPDCL to compensate M/s. Chaitanya for the energy
injected into the grid from 30.03.2017 until the eventual date of its disconnection
on 23.03.2020, calculated at a rate of ₹ 2.93 per unit. It is this limited direction
that forms the subject matter of the present appeal. The Appellants have filed the
current appeal against the later direction of the State Commission i.e. decree
under Section 70 of the Contract Act.
3. M/s. Chaitanya established a 0.8 MW wind energy project which was
commissioned on 29.03.2017. APSPDCL entered into the PPA dated 30.03.2017 with
M/s. Chaitanya.
4. Thereafter, M/s. Chaitanya continued to inject electrical energy generated
from its wind project into the grid. On 02.03.2020, APSPDCL issued a
communication to M/s. Chaitanya stating that any power supplied would be
treated as inadvertent power injected without proper consent and that no payment
would be made for the same.
5. Subsequently, on 23.03.2020, the project of M/s. Chaitanya was
completely disconnected from the grid. M/s. Chaitanya approached the State
Commission by filing O.P. No. 20 of 2020, praying for the specific performance
of the PPA and seeking payment for the power it had generated and supplied.
6. We note that similar matter for another generating company namely
Vibrant Greentech India Private Limited (VGIPL) was dealt with by the State
Commission in the same Impugned Order. APSPDCL and APPCC , which are
the Appellants in the present case had filed similar appeal bearing No. 468 of
2022 with VGIPL. On the other hand, a cross-appeal was filed by VGPIL bearing
Page 3 of 6

Judgement in Appeal No. 456 of 2022
No. 11 of 2022, which inter-alia challenged the validity of disconnection by
APSPDCL and also prayed for enhancement of the compensation granted by
the State Commission.
7. When the present appeal along with the two other appeals mentioned in
the previous paragraphs came up for hearing on 02.07.2026 before us, the
Learned Counsel appearing on behalf of APSPDCL & Andhra Pradesh Power
Coordination Committee (APPCC) which are the Appellants in present appeal as
well as in Appeal No. 468 of 2022 submitted that they have already filed written
submissions in Appeal Nos. 11 & 468 of 2022 and the same may be read as
written submission in so far as this Appeal is concerned.
8. On the other hand, Mr. Hitendra Nath Rath, Learned Counsel for VGIPL
submitted that they have already filed their written submissions in Appeal Nos.
11 & 468 of 2022. He further submitted that he has no instruction with regard to
Appeal No. 456 of 2022 is concerned. He was advised to take instructions and
submit the same by way of an affidavit within one week. Thereafter, the judgment
was reserved in Appeal No. 456 of 2022.
9. Vide Affidavit dated 08.07.2026, Mr. Hitendra Nath Rath, Learned
Counsel submitted that he had tried to contact the Respondent No. 2- M/s.
Chaitanya but there is no instruction from them.
10. The question for our determination is whether a power generator can be
awarded compensation under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 for
energy injected into a grid system under the aegis of an unapproved and legally
unenforceable PPA.
Page 4 of 6

Judgement in Appeal No. 456 of 2022
11. This Tribunal has already pronounced judgement on 07.07.2026 in that
case under Appeal No. 11 of 2022 and Appeal No. 468 of 2022. In the aforesaid
judgement, after detailed analysis, we had inter-alia upheld the decision of the
State Commission to award compensation to VGPIL under Section 70 of the
Contract Act.
12. In so far as issue of validity of the compensation granted by the State
Commission, the said matter shares an identical factual matrix, emerges from the
very same Impugned Order dated 05.07.2021 passed by the State Commission
and addresses the exact same legal issues. Therefore, in the present case also,
we uphold the decision of the State Commission to award compensation under
Section 70 of the Contract Act.
13. The related issues which naturally arises is that in the Impugned Order,
the State Commission had awarded the aforesaid compensation at the rate of ₹
2.93 per unit. As mentioned earlier, VGPIL had filed a cross appeal No. 11 of
2022 in which prayer was to increase the compensation. In that case, after
detailed analysis, we had remanded the matter to the State Commission for fresh
determination of the rate of compensation.
14. However, we note that in the present proceedings, not only there is no cross
appeal, but the Respondent No. 2 M/s. Chaitanya has neither appeared before
us, nor any submissions have been filed on their behalf.
15. Appellate courts possess wide powers under Order XLI Rule 33 of the Code
of Civil Procedure, 1908, to pass any decree or make any order which ought to
have been passed, even in favour of a party who has neither preferred an appeal
nor filed cross-objections, where the circumstances so warrant. However, the
power is discretionary and is intended to avoid inconsistent, contradictory or
Page 5 of 6

Judgement in Appeal No. 456 of 2022
unworkable decrees and to do complete justice between the parties. Since the
power under Rule 33 constitutes an exception to the general principle that a party
cannot obtain a more favourable decree without preferring an appeal or filing
cross-objections, it must be exercised with care and caution (Choudhary Sahu
(Dead) by LRs v. State of Bihar, (1982) 1 SCC 232). Ordinarily the appellate
court must not vary or reverse a decree/order in favour of a party who has not
preferred any appeal; however, in exceptional cases, the Rule enables the
appellate court to pass such decree or order as ought to have been passed (K.
Muthuswami Gounder v. N. Palaniappa Gounder, (1998) 7 SCC 327).
16. In view of the above analysis, we have consciously decided not to remand
the matter to the State Commission for fresh determination of rate of
compensation.
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons as stated above, the captioned Appeal No. 456 of 2022
is disallowed.
PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT ON THIS 16th DAY OF JULY, 2026.
(Ajay Talegaonkar) (Virender Bhat)
Technical Member Judicial Member

JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by M/s. Odisha Power Generation
Corporation Ltd. (“Appellant”/ “OPGC”) challenging the Impugned Order passed
by Odisha Electricity Regulatory Commission’s (“Respondent No. 1”/ “OERC”/
“State Commission”) Order dated 21.05.2021 in Case No. 54 of 2018 (“Impugned
Order”).
Description of the Parties
2. The Appellant is Odisha Power Generation Corporation Limited (OPGC), a
Page 3 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
generating company in terms of Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
3. Respondent No. 1 is the Odisha Electricity Regulatory Commission (OERC/
State Commission) which has been constituted under Section 3 of the Orissa
Electricity Reform Act, 1995 to perform the functions specified inter alia in Section
11 of the OER Act and Section 86 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
4. Respondent No. 2, the GRID Corporation of Odisha (GRIDCO), is a
company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and is engaged in the
business of bulk purchase and bulk sale of electricity inter alia to the four
distribution companies operating in the State of Odisha and is also a deemed
trading licensee under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The entire quantum
of electricity generated at the power plant of the Appellant-OPGC is sold to
GRIDCO under the terms of the Bulk Power Supply Agreement dated 13.08.1996
as amended by the Supplementary Agreement dated 19.12.2012.
5. Respondent Nos. 3 to 13 are pro-forma Respondents who were impleaded
before the Commission.
6. Respondent No. 14 is the Government of Odisha (GoO).
Factual Matrix of the Case
7. The Appellant owns and operates a thermal power station comprising Unit-1
and 2 of 210 MW each which commenced commercial operation in 1994 and 1996
respectively.
8. OPGC and GRIDCO entered into a Bulk Power Supply Agreement dated
13.08.1996 for sale of the entire generation from the said generating station. A
Supplementary Agreement dated 19.12.2012 was thereafter executed amending
certain terms of the original PPA.
Page 4 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
9. Disputes arose between the parties as to the basis for determination of tariff
for the generating station, namely whether tariff was to be governed by the terms
of the PPA or by the tariff regulations framed by OERC.
10. By order dated 27.04.2015 passed in Case No. 13 of 2002, the State
Commission approved the amended PPA up to 30.06.2026 and directed OPGC to
file annual tariff petitions from FY 2016-17 onwards in accordance with the
approved PPA. Prior thereto, tariff for supply of power by OPGC to GRIDCO was
being considered in GRIDCO’s ARR proceedings.
11. In GRIDCO’s ARR proceedings for FY 2012-13, the State Commission by
order dated 23.03.2012 in Case No. 91 of 2011, approved expenditure towards
installation of environmental protection equipment as part of year-end charges.
However, GRIDCO, by letter dated 16.11.2012, informed OPGC that
reimbursement of such expenditure would be considered only after approval by
the State Commission.
12. In the ARR proceedings for FY 2015-16, GRIDCO did not include certain
environmental protection expenditure projected by OPGC on the ground that the
same was subject to approval of the amended PPA. By tariff order dated
23.03.2015 in Case No. 68 of 2014, the State Commission accepted GRIDCO’s
proposal and approved year-end charges without including the said expenditure.
13. Pursuant to the order dated 27.04.2015 in Case No. 13 of 2002, OPGC filed
Petition being Case No. 53 of 2015 for determination of tariff for FY 2016-17. In
the said petition, OPGC claimed additional capitalisation of about ₹ 95.65 crore,
comprising expenditure incurred during FYs 2014-15 and 2015-16 and projected
expenditure for FY 2016-17.
Page 5 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
14. By order dated 21.03.2016 in Case No. 53 of 2015, the State Commission
declined to allow the claim for additional capitalisation on the ground that OPGC
had not furnished details of the works executed and use of the assets and that the
audited accounts did not recognise the proposed capitalisation. The State
Commission, however, observed that expenditure incurred during FY 2015-16, if
otherwise in accordance with the applicable regulations could be considered in
subsequent years.
15. Aggrieved thereby, OPGC filed Appeal No. 126 of 2016 before this Tribunal.
In the said appeal, OPGC had contended that the tariff norms contained in the
approved and amended PPA, and consequent Supplemental Agreement executed
pursuant to the Government of Odisha Notification would govern the determination
of tariff and not the OERC Tariff Regulations. This appeal came to be dismissed
by judgment dated 06.04.2017 wherein this Tribunal had concluded that the
Regulations framed by the State Commission have primacy. This judgement was
thereafter assailed by OPGC before the Hon’ble Supreme Court.
16. During the pendency of Appeal No. 126 of 2016, OPGC filed Case No. 62 of
2016 for determination of tariff for FY 2017-18. In support of its claim for additional
capitalisation of about ₹ 96.51 crore, OPGC placed on record documents including
work orders, vendor bills and auditor certificates.
17. By order dated 23.03.2017 in Case No. 62 of 2016, the State Commission
again declined to allow the claim for additional capitalisation, holding that
documentary evidence regarding installation and utilisation of the assets had not
been produced and that the regulations did not contemplate approval of projected
future expenditure as additional capitalisation.
18. Thereafter, OPGC filed Civil Appeal No. 9485 of 2017 before the Hon’ble
Supreme Court challenging the judgment of this Tribunal dated 06.04.2017.
Page 6 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
19. OPGC filed Case No. 75 of 2017 seeking determination of tariff for FY 2018-
19. By order dated 22.03.2018 in Case No. 75 of 2017, the State Commission
observed that the issue of additional capitalisation required separate examination
and directed that the same be considered through a separate application.
20. On 19.04.2018, the Hon’ble Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 9485
of 2017, set aside the judgment of this Tribunal and remanded the matter to the
State Commission with directions to determine tariff by applying the Government
Notification dated 21.06.2008 for fixed costs, the PPA for variable costs specified
therein and the applicable statutory regulations for costs not reflected in the PPA.
21. Pursuant thereto, OPGC filed Case No. 33 of 2018 seeking redetermination
of tariff for FYs 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19. OPGC also filed a separate
petition, being Case No. 54 of 2018, seeking approval of additional capitalisation
in respect of expenditure incurred during FYs 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18,
projected expenditure for FY 2018-19 and carrying cost thereon. OPGC continued
to raise claims relating to additional capitalisation in its subsequent annual tariff
petitions for FYs 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22.
22. By order dated 28.03.2019 passed in Case No. 33 of 2018, the State
Commission re-determined tariff in terms of the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme
Court. While noting that the petition for additional capitalisation was pending
separately, the State Commission did not consider the said claim in the tariff
redetermination proceedings. Similar observations were made by the State
Commission in the tariff orders for FYs 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22.
23. By order dated 21.05.2021 passed in Case No. 54 of 2018, the State
Commission rejected OPGC’s claim for additional capitalisation.
24. Subsequently, OPGC also filed Case No. 66 of 2021 before the State
Page 7 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
Commission seeking approval for renovation and modernisation of the generating
station including life extension works and installation of Flue Gas Desulphurisation
(FGD) system.
25. Aggrieved by the order dated 21.05.2021 passed in Case No. 54 of 2018
rejecting its claim for additional capitalisation, OPGC has preferred the present
appeal.
26. The Appellant has prayed for the following relief before us:
“(a) Admit the present Appeal and set aside the Impugned Order dated
21.05.2021 passed by the Ld. Odisha Electricity Regulatory Commission in Case
No. 54 of 2018;
(b) Declare that the Appellant is entitled to claim additional capitalisation from
FY 2015-16 onwards in terms of the Ld. Commission’s extant regulations and allow
the claims made by Appellant in Case No. 54 o 2018 and subsequent annual tariff
petitions, by way of pass through in tariff;
(c) Direct Respondent No. 2, GRIDCO to forthwith pay to the Appellant all
legitimate dues on account of the Appellant’s additional capitalisation claims;
(d) Award the Appellant interest and associated carrying costs;
(e) Award the Appellant costs; and
(f) pass such other and further orders/ directions as this Hon’ble Tribunal may
deem just and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
Submissions of the Appellant-OPGC
27. OPGC submitted that OERC wrongly denied OPGC’s Additional
Capitalisation claims from FY 2015-16 onwards by incorrectly holding that no such
claim can be made during the PPA period.
28. The Supreme Court’s 19.04.2018 judgment was misread; it preserved the
applicability of statutory OERC Regulations for “other costs” not covered by the
Page 8 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
PPA and Additional Capitalisation falls in that category.
29. Neither the PPA nor the 2008 GoO Notification freezes Capital Cost or bars
Additional Capitalisation; OERC wrongly conflated capital cost, tariff norms and
AFC components.
30. The Odisha Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for
Determination of Generation Tariff) Regulations, 2014 (“2014 Tariff Regulations”)
expressly permit Additional Capitalisation subject to prudence check and OERC
could not override these binding regulations by relying on the PPA/GoO
Notification.
31. OERC wrongly treated Additional Capitalisation as O&M/ future R&M
expenditure even though these are distinct statutory heads; OERC’s own later
orders allowing R&M/ FGD/ ash-pond costs show inconsistency in its stand.
32. No prior approval is required unless the Regulations expressly say so; the
only test is whether the expenditure fits within the regulatory heads and passes
prudence check.
33. OPGC submitted that the impugned order is also vitiated by a 19-month
delay in pronouncement and if the claims are allowed, OPGC is also entitled to
carrying cost for the period of under-recovery.
Submissions of the Respondent No. 1- OERC
34. OERC submitted that the Appellant’s petition was deficient and incomplete
as it lacked essential data, justification, original scope of work, CEA approval and
a Remaining Life Assessment (RLA) study; therefore, the Commission rightly
permitted the Appellant to re-approach only after curing these defects.
Page 9 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
35. Additional Capitalisation cannot be allowed as a matter of course under the
2014 Regulations; it is subject to prudence check and compliance with Regulations
3.3 and 3.4 which the Appellant failed to satisfy.
36. OERC further submitted that the Appellant did not comply with mandatory
statutory preconditions, including prior approval from OERC, adequate supporting
justification and material particulars of the proposed capital works.
37. OERC correctly distinguished between O&M expenses, R&M expenses and
Additional Capitalisation, each of which is governed by a separate regulatory
framework and the Appellant wrongly mixed up these concepts.
38. The Commission decided the matter in accordance with the 2008
Government Notification, the PPA and the 2014 OERC Regulations and the
Appellant’s argument that these were ignored is incorrect.
39. OERC submitted that the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated
19.04.2018 did not entitle the Appellant to Additional Capitalisation but left it to the
State Commission to decide the issue on facts and in accordance with law.
40. RLA was essential because there were conflicting positions on the useful life
of the generating station; 25 years under the Regulations, 30 years under the PPA
and an even longer period under the Fuel Supply Agreement and without clarity
on remaining life, the claim could not be examined properly.
41. OERC further submitted that since the station’s PLAF had drastically
reduced during FY 2015-16 to FY 2018-19 and the Appellant is a Government
undertaking, allowing such claims without compliance with statutory requirements
would risk wastage of public money and impose an additional burden on
consumers.
Page 10 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
Submissions of the Respondent No. 2 - GRIDCO
42. GRIDCO submitted that the Additional Capitalisation was not justified at the
end of the plant’s life; Units 1 and 2 were commissioned in 1994 and 1996 and
were to reach the end of useful life by June 2026; OPGC also failed to submit the
mandatory RLA study especially when continuation itself depended on FGD
compliance under environmental norms.
43. The 2008 GoO Notification freezes the Fixed Cost / capital structure and the
Hon’ble Supreme Court’s 2018 judgment did not permit alteration of that capital
base; therefore, any expenditure which expands the capital base could not be
allowed as Additional Capitalisation and had to be absorbed within the relaxed
O&M framework under the PPA.
44. GRIDCO further submitted that the expenditure did not improve plant
performance; despite spending ₹ 122.15 crore, the PLF declined (86.01% in 2016-
17, 74.18% in 2017-18, 82.42% in 2018-19 and 69.73% in 2019-20) showing that
the expenses were in the nature of routine O&M or R&M, not true Additional
Capitalisation.
45. OPGC failed to obtain prior approval and failed to furnish records including
the original project report and scope of work, hence it could not be verified whether
items such as ash pond height extension were genuinely additional or already
covered within the original project cost of ₹ 1,060 crores.
46. GRIDCO submitted that OPGC already enjoyed relaxed norms under the
PPA for Units 1 and 2; such as favourable norms for recovery of fixed charges,
incentives, specific fuel oil consumption, auxiliary consumption, station heat rate
and O&M escalation and therefore any further expenditure should be met within
that framework rather than through tariff loading.
Page 11 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
47. Under Clause 12.4 of the original PPA read with the MoP Notification dated
30.03.1992, the capital cost was subject to a ceiling of ₹ 1,060 crores and since
the units were already fully depreciated by 2012 and loans liquidated by 2009,
loading fresh capital costs on a plant nearing closure would cause an abnormal
tariff increase.
48. In any event, OPGC later itself sought and obtained a separate R&M/ life-
extension package in Case No. 66 of 2021 where it admitted severe forced
outages and declining efficiency, obtained in-principle approval of ₹ 756.84 crore
for R&M and FGD by order dated 03.11.2021 and later secured approval of ₹ 140
crores for a new ash pond in Review Petition Case No. 99 of 2021 by order dated
15.01.2022.
49. Therefore, according to GRIDCO, the capital requirements of Units 1 and 2
already stand addressed under the approved R&M/ life-extension framework and
any remaining expenditure claimed in the present proceedings should be borne by
OPGC out of the relaxed O&M expenses under the PPA, not through Additional
Capitalisation.
Analysis and Conclusion
50. We have perused the Impugned Order. The relevant part of the order, which
covers the reasoning of the State Commission for rejecting the prayer for additional
capitalization is extracted below:
“32. The Commission heard the parties. As per judgement of Hon’ble Supreme
Court dated 19.04.2018 the norms for variable cost shall be as per PPA and
the notification of the State Government dated 21.06.2008 shall be used for
fixed cost. For other costs not reflected in the PPA, the statutory Regulation
may be applied. The two power generating units have been in operation since
1994 and 1996 respectively. They will complete their useful life by the year
2026 unless it is extended as per PPA. The Petitioner has also not submitted
the Residual Life Assessment study. Therefore, a few years are left for life of
the power plant to come to an end. If FGD is not installed then power station
Page 12 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
shall be phased out much earlier as per the MOEF guideline. As per the
judgement of Hon’ble Supreme Court from the point of view of fixed cost the
Government notification dated 21.06.2008 is only to be considered. However,
Hon’ble Court has given relaxation in the variable cost by mentioning that if
anything is not reflected in the PPA then statutory Regulation shall apply.
Proposal for additional capitalisation as submitted by the Petitioner shall have
impact on the fixed cost of the power station. However, this has been frozen
by Government notification which has been concurred by Hon’ble Supreme
Court. Therefore, it is not possible on our part to consider expenditure incurred
by the Petitioner in different areas as additional capitalisation rather they
would come under relaxed O&M norms of PPA. After incurring the expenditure
of Rs.122.15 crore the PLF of the plant has not improved substantially which
can be seen from the following table.
Year PLF
2016-17 86.01%
2017-18 74.18%
2018-19 82.42%

51. It may be seen from the above extract that the State Commission had
rejected the prayer of OPGC for additional capitalization on the following grounds:
(i) Based on their interpretation of the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court
in Civil Appeal No. 9485 of 2017
(ii) The expenditure is of the nature of operation and maintenance
(iii) Prior approval was not sought, and
(iv) Original project report is not available to justify the present work
52. In its submissions, GRIDCO has supported the aforesaid conclusion of the
State Commission in the Impugned Order. We now take up these grounds one by
one. We shall first address ground (ii), as it is foundational. If the expenditure is
found not to be capital in nature, the other grounds need not be examined.
Generally, meaning of capital expenditure is well understood. Although the General
Financial Rules, 20171 of Government of India do not govern the present
controversy, the distinction drawn between capital expenditure and revenue
expenditure in Rule 84 thereof may be usefully referred to by way of illustration:
“Significant expenditure incurred with the object of acquiring tangible assets of
a permanent nature (for use in the organisation and not for sale in the ordinary
course of business) or enhancing the utility of existing assets, shall broadly be
defined as Capital expenditure.
Subsequent charges on maintenance, repair, upkeep and working expenses,
which are required to maintain the assets in a running order as also all other
expenses incurred for the day to day running of the organisation, including
establishment and administrative expenses shall be classified as Revenue
expenditure.”
53. It can be seen that the State Commission has examined this issue solely
from the standpoint of efficiency improvement, which, cannot by itself be the
criterion for an expenditure to qualify as capital expenditure. Further, an
improvement in PLF is not a measure of efficiency. PLF is a measure of the plant’s

the capacity, efficiency, or useful life of an existing asset. Therefore, we do not
agree with the conclusion of the State Commission that since PLF has not
improved, the claim is of the nature of operation and maintenance expense.
54. Coming to the ground (iii), we have also perused the OERC Regulations,
2014 and we could not find requirement of prior approval in the relevant

Regulation 3.3 and 3.4. This is also submission of the OPGC. Therefore, we are

55. As regards ground (iv), we find that Regulation 3.3 of the OERC Regulations,
2014 is relevant, and is extracted below:
“3.3 The capital expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred, on the

56. It is evident from the first proviso to the above extracted Regulation that the
submission of the original scope of work is a mandatory requirement. The rationale
is self-evident. In the absence of these particulars, it would be difficult, if not
impossible, to determine whether the asset or item for which additional
capitalisation is sought was originally envisaged within the approved scope of work
and merely remained unexecuted at the relevant point of time, or whether it
constitutes an altogether new item. Therefore, the State Commission was justified
in faulting the OPGC for its failure to submit the original scope of work.
57. Now the main ground for rejection of the claim appears to be ground (i),
which is based on the interpretation of the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court.
The question, however, is whether the interpretation adopted by them, and the
conclusion drawn therefrom, are correct. The relevant extract of the order of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 19.04.2018 in CA No. 9485 of 2017 is reproduced
below:
“7. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order and remand the matter
to the State Commission for fresh decision. The State Commission may take
into account the Notification dated 21.06.2008| for the fixed costs, the PPA for
the variable costs specified therein and for other costs not reflected in the PPA,
statutory Regulations may be applied.”
58. It is clear that Hon’ble Supreme Court in its direction has mentioned three
types of costs- fixed costs, variable costs and other costs. The State Commission
has interpreted third limb of the direction as relaxation given by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in the variable cost. In other words, the State Commission has
Page 16 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
interpreted that the words “other costs” as mentioned by the Hon’ble Supreme
Court, is part of variable costs not reflected in the PPA. In our opinion, this
interpretation has a problem. The interpretation of the State Commission
effectively reads the sentence as if it says “...for other variable costs not reflected
in the PPA...”. However, the word “variable” does not appear before “other costs”
in the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court. It is settled position that one should not
read words into a judgment that are not there unless necessary to give effect to
the evident intention. One may argue that because Hon’ble Supreme Court first
says “Government notification ... for the fixed costs,” all fixed costs are already
exhausted by that source, the third category cannot include fixed costs. However,
in our opinion this is not the case. Hon’ble Supreme Court has only directed that
the State Commission may “take into account” the notification issued by the
Government. The intention of the direction seems to be that while determining the
fixed costs, the State Commission has to rely primarily on Government notification,
but the same is not mechanically binding in every conceivable situation. Thus, we
are of the opinion that the “other costs not reflected in the PPA” is a separate,
residual category, not a subset of “variable costs”. The purpose of the third limb
appears to avoid precisely a gap that may arise by application of the Government
Notification for fixed costs and PPA for variable costs. Therefore, the third limb
covers both fixed and variable costs. Examples of such “other costs”, by way of
illustration and not limitation, could include SLDC fees and charges, water cess,
regulatory expenses, and similar costs that perhaps may arise but were not in
vogue when the PPA was executed. Thus, our interpretation of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court order is:
(i) Fixed costs: To be determine by the State Commission taking into account
the Government notification.
(ii) Variable costs: To be expressly covered by the PPA

(iii) Other costs (could be fixed or variable): which are not dealt with by the
PPA, are to be dealt with according to the regulations of the State
Commission.
59. Further, in our opinion the word “costs” hear refers to heads of cost or cost
elements and not the monitory amount for a cost element. This is because in the
order, Hon’ble Supreme Court was dealing with the question as to which
instrument governs which kind of cost; and not with the question as to how much
should be allowed. Secondly, Hon’ble Supreme Court has used the phrase “as
reflected in the PPA”. If the intent was to refer to monitory amount, the phrase could
have been “as fixed/ agreed/ quantified in the PPA”.
60. Now, the “additional capitalisation” is not a separate cost element but if
allowed, it only adds to the “capital cost”. We see that in the PPA as executed in
1996 (in supersession to the earlier PPA of 1991), besides fixing other parameters,
the capital cost is fixed at ₹ 1060 Cr, the capital cost for arriving at O&M expenses
(as 2.5% of the capital cost) for the first year has been pegged at ₹ 1030 Cr, and
the escalation in O&M expenses had been pegged at 8%. Generally, when PPA is
executed before or during construction, there is a provision that capital cost shall
be actual or agreed whichever is less. However, this has not been the case with
this PPA. Similarly, there is standard practice of linking escalation in O&M
expenses to some index; this was also the case in the then prevailing GOI tariff
notification issued on 30th March 1992. However, in this case the escalation has
been pegged at 8% per annum, which according to GRIDCO is on higher side.
Therefore, the PPA executed in 1996 seems to be part of a negotiated settlement
to minimise the uncertainty in any of the elements of tariff.
61. Further, there is no specific mention of additional capital expenditure in the
original PPA, Government notification dated 21.06.2008 and the modifications
made in the PPA consequent to aforesaid Government notification. OPGC in its

cost is not a parameter for tariff determination is inconsistent with the express
terms of the PPA. Although this contention may reflect the general practice, the
parties in the present case consciously departed from that practice by expressly
identifying capital cost as a tariff parameter and by stipulating its value in the PPA.
Not only that but the paragraph 3 (a) of the Government of Odisha notification

dated 21.06.2008 after modifying the norm for calculation of incentives from PLF

determination of tariff till validity of the PPA not withstanding modification in tariff

an independent category of cost. Upon approval, it is absorbed into and forms part
of the capital cost. Therefore, the submission of OPGC that additional capital

of the Hon’ble Supreme Court is misconceived and cannot be accepted.
63. Further, it is clear from the Government of Odisha notification dated
21.06.2008 (paragraph 2) that in order to resolve the dispute regarding tariff setting
for the Units #1 & 2 and other related matters, a task force was constituted by the
Government of Odisha. To be specific, the dispute was about amendment to the
PPA as per “CERC guidelines” (paragraph 1 of the aforesaid notification). It is
matter of record that 49% equity in this power station was divested through
competitive bidding in the late 1990’s. We were given to understand during the
course of the hearing that since CERC tariff norms are set for each control period,
this was viewed as source of uncertainty by the foreign investor. From para ix) of
the recital of the supplemental agreement dated 19.12.2012 (effective from
01.04.2007), it is clear that changes made in the PPA were part of overall
settlement of all the disputes and differences.
64. The underlying premise appears to be that the Government of Odisha
notification dated 21.06.2008 and consequent Supplemental PPA were part of a
well thought commercial settlement. While the tariff parameters, including the
capital cost, were frozen, thereby precluding any future increase in tariff on account
of additional capitalization, the tariff continued to be governed by the existing
norms and was not subjected to the more stringent operational and financial norms
that may get introduced under the subsequent CERC Tariff Notifications (which act
as guideline to the State Commission in accordance with Section 61 (a) of the

65. However, we must point that the provisions of PPA, including the freeze on
tariff parameters does not appear to be cast in stone. The Supplemental PPA
leaves doors open for taking care of contingencies with fairness and without
detriment to interest of any party. The paragraph E) of the Supplemental PPA,
which records this understanding is extracted below:
“E) In the PPA the following clause be added as 17.01

endeavours to remove the cause or causes of the same: It is hereby agreed that

66. OPGC has placed reliance on the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court
in PTC India Limited v. CERC, (2010) 4 SCC 603, to contend that the regulations
framed under the Electricity Act, 2003 constitute binding subordinate legislation.
While there can be no quarrel with this proposition, the present case stands on a
different footing. The issue in question has already been adjudicated by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in proceedings between the same parties. In this
judgement, Hon’ble Supreme Court had set aside judgement of this Tribunal,
which was based on the principle that the regulations prevail over agreement as
laid down in the PTC cited above. The judgment, rendered by the Hon’ble Supreme
Court after considering the relevant facts and circumstances, including the
Government of Odisha Notification, contains specific directions governing the

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
rights and obligations of the parties. Accordingly, the adjudication by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court on the issue operates as res judicata between the parties, and the
directions contained therein are binding upon them. Consequently, the matter
cannot be reopened by placing reliance on the general proposition regarding the
binding nature of statutory regulations.
67. OPGC has also pointed out that later, OERC vide Order dated 03.11.2021 in
Case No. 66 of 2021 and Order dated 15.01.2022 in Case No. 99 of 2021 itself
has allowed additional expenditure on R&M, FGD and on ash pond expenditure
for OPGC’s Units 1 and 2; and has contended this to be as inconsistent stand of
the State Commission. Though, we would like to refrain from passing any remark
on the aforesaid orders since these orders are not subject matter of the current
proceedings, from the submissions of the GRDICO and a glance at these orders
which are on record, prima facie it appears that in the proceeding before the State
Commission, GRIDCO had consented for expenditure on R&M and FGD, which is
in the spirit of the paragraph E) of the Supplemental PPA referred earlier. Further,
it appears that the expenditure on ash pond were approved by OERC as a
consequence to change in law.
68. OPGC has placed reliance on this Tribunal’s judgment dated 28.08.2023 in
Appeal No. 304 of 2016 & batch (NTPC Limited v. CERC & Ors.), wherein it was
held that additional capitalization, renovation and modernisation (R&M), special
allowance and the normative components of Annual Fixed Charges (AFC)
constitute distinct statutory concepts under the applicable tariff regulations. On that
basis, OPGC contends that the OERC could not have rejected its statutory claim
for additional capitalization.
69. In our considered view, the said judgment is distinguishable on facts and has
no application to the present case. The controversy before us arises in a materially
different factual and legal setting, where the rights and obligations of the parties
Page 22 of 24

Judgement in Appeal No. 335 of 2021
are governed by the terms of the PPA, which expressly freezes the capital cost,
read in conjunction with the specific directions contained in the judgment of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has, after considering the
Government Notification and the contractual framework, delineated the respective
instruments governing different categories of costs. In these peculiar
circumstances, the general principles enunciated in the judgment relied upon by
OPGC cannot override the binding contractual arrangement and the specific
adjudication of the Hon’ble Supreme Court governing the parties.
70. For the foregoing reasons, we hold that the pegging of the capital cost for
the purpose of tariff determination constituted an essential element of the
negotiated settlement embodied in the PPA. Any subsequent allowance of
additional capitalization, leading to an increase in tariff, would alter the contractual
allocation of risks and benefits reflected in that settlement. We, therefore, affirm
the conclusion reached by the State Commission, albeit for a reason different from
that assigned by it.
71. Before parting with the matter, we consider it appropriate to observe upon
one further aspect. As noticed earlier, it was submitted during the course of
hearing that the constitution of the Task Force, culminating in the issuance of the
Notification by the Government of Odisha and the execution of the Supplemental
Agreement, was primarily intended to provide tariff certainty to the foreign investor.
We were also given to understand that the foreign investor has since divested its
equity holding and that the Government of Odisha now holds the entire equity in
the Power Station. In the aforesaid circumstances, the rationale, if any, for the
continuance of any special dispensation in favour of the said generating station
appears to have substantially ceased to exist. The continuance of such special
treatment may not only give rise to otherwise avoidable disputes on account of
differing interpretations, as demonstrated in the present proceedings, but may also
be inconsistent with the scheme and underlying spirit of the Electricity Act, 2003.

Accordingly, we observe that it would be open to the parties to bring this aspect to
the notice of the Government of Odisha so that it may examine the matter and, if
considered appropriate, take suitable steps to review the continuance of any
special dispensation applicable to the Power Station.
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons as stated above, we have come to the conclusion that
the State Commission was right in disallowing the additional capitalisation and
accordingly the captioned Appeal No. 335 of 2021 is disallowed.
The Captioned Appeal and pending IAs, if any, are disposed of in the above terms.
